# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to melt lead, while the nightside plunges to hundreds of degrees below zero, potentially freezing atmospheres onto the surface. Yet this stark division doesn't necessarily render such worlds uninhabitable.

Atmospheric circulation becomes the great equalizer. On tidally locked planets, winds transport heat from the dayside to the nightside, moderating temperatures on both sides. A global ocean could distribute heat efficiently, potentially creating a narrow ring of habitability near the terminator—the twilight zone between day and night.
